concepts.caption: Run the strategy over old data and see what it would have done.
concepts.definition: Simulating a strategy on historical data to estimate its return and risk.
concepts.example: We backtest a simple momentum overlay on a universe of ten energy futures.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A backtest is the experiment; overfitting is a disease the experiment can catch.

concepts.caption: The stretch of data you tuned the parameters on.
concepts.definition: The period used to fit or optimise a model, where results are optimistic by construction.
concepts.example: In-sample, from 2010 to 2019, the strategy produces a Sharpe of 1.4.
concepts.mixUpWhy: In-sample is the data you tuned on, so it flatters; out-of-sample is untouched and shows what generalises.

concepts.caption: The stretch you never touched, held back for the test.
concepts.definition: Data excluded from fitting and tuning, used to test whether a strategy generalises.
concepts.example: Out-of-sample, from 2020 to 2024, the Sharpe falls to 0.4.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Out-of-sample is untouched and tests generalisation; in-sample was tuned and tests fit.

concepts.caption: Refit each year on what was knowable then, trade the next year.
concepts.definition: A validation method that rolls forward in time, refitting on past data only — the closest simulation of live constraints.
concepts.example: A walk-forward test produces a Sharpe of 0.6, between the two.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Walk-forward is a backtest with time discipline (only past data each step); a plain backtest can peek at the future.

concepts.caption: The yardstick you are measured against.
concepts.definition: The index or strategy used as the reference for judging whether active management added value.
concepts.example: Alpha against the benchmark is 4.2% a year.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A benchmark is what you are compared to; a universe is what you pick from.

concepts.caption: Tuned until it fits the noise, not the signal.
concepts.definition: Fitting a model so closely to past data that it captures random variation and breaks on new data.
concepts.example: The drop is what you expect when a specification is overfitting the first decade.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Overfitting is the model hugging noise (the result); data snooping is the repeated searching that gets you there (the cause).

concepts.caption: Deciding with data that was not published yet.
concepts.definition: Using information published after the decision point in a backtest, which inflates returns.
concepts.example: Look-ahead bias appears if a signal uses data published after the decision point.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Look-ahead bias cheats on time; survivorship bias cheats on the sample.

concepts.caption: Counting only what survived, ignoring what died.
concepts.definition: A sample containing only currently existing assets, dropping those delisted or closed, which flatters results.
concepts.example: Survivorship bias appears if the universe is taken from today's list of contracts.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Survivorship bias is the wrong sample (only survivors); look-ahead bias is the wrong time (the future).

concepts.caption: Rummaging through one dataset until something looks significant.
concepts.definition: Testing hypotheses repeatedly on the same data until a statistically significant result appears by chance, then treating it as a finding.
concepts.example: Data snooping appears if we try many variants and report the best.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Data snooping is the habit of hunting; multiple testing is the statistical consequence that produces the false positives.

concepts.caption: Run many tests and false positives show up on schedule.
concepts.definition: The statistical fact that the chance of at least one false positive rises with the number of tests run on one dataset.
concepts.example: At a 5% level, twenty independent tests produce roughly one false positive by construction.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Multiple testing is the statistical fact; data snooping is how that fact gets exploited.

concepts.caption: Return earned per unit of the bumpiness endured.
concepts.definition: Excess return divided by return volatility — the reward per unit of risk taken.
concepts.example: In-sample the strategy produces a Sharpe ratio of 1.4.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Sharpe looks at average volatility (how smooth the ride was); max drawdown looks at the single worst fall. A high Sharpe can still hide a deep drawdown.

concepts.caption: The deepest fall from a peak.
concepts.definition: The largest decline from a peak to the subsequent trough — the worst loss actually suffered.
concepts.example: The maximum drawdown widens to 31% out of sample.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Max drawdown is the deepest fall that actually happened; VaR is an estimated threshold from a distribution.

concepts.caption: How many trades made money, as a share of all trades.
concepts.definition: The share of trades that were profitable.
concepts.example: The hit rate is 54%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Hit rate counts trades; expectancy weighs how much each win and loss was worth. A high hit rate with negative expectancy is common.

concepts.caption: What an average trade is worth.
concepts.definition: The expected profit or loss per trade: win rate times average win, minus loss rate times average loss.
concepts.example: The expectancy per trade is 0.6%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Expectancy is weighted by size; hit rate only counts frequency.

concepts.caption: The part left over after the market's contribution is removed.
concepts.definition: Risk-adjusted excess return over a benchmark — the strategy's own contribution.
concepts.example: Alpha against the benchmark is 4.2% a year.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Alpha is the excess over the benchmark (skill); beta is how much of the market you carry (exposure).

concepts.caption: How much you move when the market moves one percent.
concepts.definition: An asset's systematic exposure to the market, measuring sensitivity to market moves.
concepts.example: With a beta of 0.35, most of the return is not explained by market exposure.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Beta is exposure (how much you ride the market); alpha is what is left after that exposure is accounted for.

concepts.caption: How far your return drifts from the benchmark's.
concepts.definition: The volatility of the difference between portfolio and benchmark returns — how much you deviate.
concepts.example: Tracking error against the benchmark is 6.5% a year.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Tracking error measures deviation regardless of direction; alpha measures the directional part you keep.

concepts.caption: The set you are allowed to pick from.
concepts.definition: The collection of assets a strategy may invest in, which sets its boundaries and bias risk.
concepts.example: We backtest on a universe of the ten largest energy futures.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The universe is where you pick from; the benchmark is what you are compared to.

concepts.caption: Drag the holdings back to their target weights.
concepts.definition: Adjusting holdings back to target weights on a schedule or rule.
concepts.example: We rebalance monthly at 12% one-way turnover.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Rebalancing is the act of restoring weights; turnover is how much trading that act required.

concepts.caption: How much money each position gets.
concepts.definition: Deciding how much capital each trade or holding receives — the direct driver of risk exposure.
concepts.example: Position sizing is capped well below the notional the backtest implies.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Position sizing is the decision of how much to put on; exposure is what you actually ended up carrying. Sizing at 10% can still expose you to more or less than 10% depending on volatility.

concepts.caption: How much of the portfolio gets replaced.
concepts.definition: Trading volume relative to portfolio size over a period — the direct driver of transaction cost.
concepts.example: At 12% one-way turnover, costs reach about 1.3% a year.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Turnover is how much is traded; transaction cost is what that trading costs.

concepts.caption: Whether two things move together.
concepts.definition: The statistical association between two assets' returns, from -1 to 1.
concepts.example: Correlation across the ten contracts is high, around 0.7.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Correlation is how much two assets move together; exposure is how much risk you carry in one.

concepts.caption: How much risk you are actually carrying.
concepts.definition: The degree to which a portfolio is sensitive to, or concentrated in, a given risk factor.
concepts.example: Most of the return is not explained by market exposure.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Exposure is what you ended up carrying; position sizing is the decision that produced it.

concepts.caption: What the buying and selling itself costs.
concepts.definition: Costs incurred in trading: commissions, bid-ask spread and taxes.
concepts.example: With 6 basis points of transaction cost per side, costs reach 1.3% a year.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Transaction cost is the visible fee (commission, spread); slippage is the gap between the price you wanted and the price you got.

concepts.caption: How much worse your fill was than the price you wanted.
concepts.definition: The difference between the intended and executed price, caused by market impact and delay.
concepts.example: Doubling slippage removes the edge entirely.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Slippage is a price gap (implicit); transaction cost is the explicit fee.

concepts.caption: The most money the strategy can hold.
concepts.definition: The maximum capital a strategy can absorb before trading costs consume the return.
concepts.example: A capacity constraint this tight means the strategy cannot absorb meaningful capital.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Capacity is how much the strategy can hold; the liquidity constraint is how much the market can trade. The second causes the first.

concepts.caption: Not enough volume in the market to trade the size.
concepts.definition: A limit imposed by insufficient market depth, making the intended size or price unreachable.
concepts.example: The liquidity constraint binds at roughly $40 million.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The liquidity constraint is a property of the market's depth; the capacity constraint is the strategy-level ceiling it produces.

concepts.caption: Replay the worst historical moment and see what happens.
concepts.definition: Evaluating a portfolio under an extreme but plausible scenario to probe tail risk.
concepts.example: A stress test on the 2020 oil crash shows the overlay loses 14% in that month.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A stress test is one extreme scenario (often a real past one); scenario analysis compares several hypothetical paths.

concepts.caption: Assume several futures and run each one.
concepts.definition: Evaluating a strategy under several assumed paths to compare outcomes across environments.
concepts.example: We run a scenario analysis on three paths.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Scenario analysis compares several hypothetical paths; a stress test is a single extreme shock.

concepts.caption: The loss you should not exceed on a given share of days.
concepts.definition: The maximum expected loss over a holding period at a given confidence level.
concepts.example: Value at risk at the 95% level is 2.1% daily.
concepts.mixUpWhy: VaR is a threshold not exceeded 95% of the time; max drawdown is the deepest fall that actually happened. VaR routinely understates tail risk.

concepts.caption: How much the answer moves when an assumption moves.
concepts.definition: The degree to which a result responds to a change in a parameter or assumption.
concepts.example: The result is sensitive to the cost assumption.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Sensitivity measures 'what if this changes'; robustness is the conclusion about whether the result still stands.

concepts.caption: Does the conclusion hold if you change the assumptions?
concepts.definition: The degree to which a strategy stays effective when parameters, samples or assumptions change.
concepts.example: A robustness check shows the sign holds in most but not all windows.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Robustness is the overall verdict (does it hold); sensitivity is the measurement that gets you there.

prompts.story: Our backtest returned 18% a year before fees and slippage. Investors should expect 18% net in live trading.
prompts.stem: Which step from historical results to live expectations is flawed?

options.text: Annual returns should be replaced by the sum of all yearly returns.
Simulated returns before costs are being treated as expected live net returns.
Any backtest covering ten years must use monthly returns.
Adding maximum drawdown would establish the expected live net return.

prompts.why: Before fees and slippage is a gross figure; net is after costs. These are different measures. Even a cost-adjusted backtest does not guarantee future returns.

prompts.story: We tuned the model on 2015-2024 data. Its Sharpe on that same period is 1.4, which we present as independent validation.
prompts.stem: Why is this not independent validation?

options.text: A positive Sharpe means the model must have too few parameters.
Ten years of data cannot be used to train any model.
Evaluation reuses the period used to tune the model.
Validation becomes independent only if the Sharpe exceeds 2.

prompts.why: Same period is the clue: the data already influenced parameter selection. The in-sample Sharpe can be reported with that label, but independent evidence needs data not used for selection.

prompts.story: We checked the holdout every week and changed the model whenever its holdout Sharpe fell. The final holdout Sharpe is 1.2.
prompts.stem: What would provide more independent evidence next?

options.text: Freeze the model and test it on new, unseen data.
Keep changing the model until its Sharpe on this holdout rises.
Simply rename the same holdout out-of-sample.
Check monthly instead, while continuing to tune on the same holdout.

prompts.why: A holdout that repeatedly guides model changes becomes selection data. Freeze the rules before using fresh unseen data. Renaming the old holdout or checking it less often cannot undo that reuse.

prompts.story: Our walk-forward test refits each January using the full 2010-2024 dataset, then simulates trades for that year, including 2018.
prompts.stem: Which change restores the time constraint of walk-forward testing?

options.text: Include more future years in each fit to stabilize parameters.
Refit monthly but keep using the full dataset.
Shuffle the full dataset before simulating each year's trades.
Fit only on data already available before each trading period.

prompts.why: At the start of 2018, data from 2019-2024 was unavailable. Walk-forward testing advances through time: fit on information available then, and evaluate on the following period. Periodic refitting alone is not enough.

prompts.story: An equity strategy reports total returns including dividends. Its benchmark uses the same index's price return, excluding dividends. The gap is called added value.
prompts.stem: Which measurement issue should be fixed first for a fair comparison?

options.text: Exclude dividends from the strategy but keep calling it total return.
Choose a lower-return index to widen the gap.
Use a benchmark with matching dates and dividend treatment, and clarify costs.
Compare only the best year to avoid the effect of dividends.

prompts.why: The strategy includes dividends while the price-return benchmark excludes them. The gap may reflect mismatched measures. Match dates and dividend treatment and state cost assumptions before discussing added value.

prompts.story: We need a historical test that refits annually while respecting what was known at each decision date. Which design should we use?
prompts.stem: Which procedure best meets the requirement?

options.text: Choose parameters on all history and label each year out-of-sample.
Fit on data available before each year, trade that year under fixed rules, then combine results.
Use each year's returns to choose parameters and backfill that year's trades.
Shuffle years so future years enter every training set.

prompts.why: Walk-forward testing fits on the past before evaluating the next period. Combine those test results without using a period's own returns to retroactively select its parameters. This design still does not guarantee future profits.

prompts.story: We tried 2,000 parameter sets on the same ten years and report only the winner: 41% a year. This proves a persistent edge.
prompts.stem: What key evidence is missing from this conclusion?

options.text: Performance on data not used to select the parameters.
A lower return for the runner-up on the same data.
A higher winning return after expanding the search to 4,000 sets.
The same 41% when the winning parameters are rerun on identical data.

prompts.why: Selecting the best of many attempts creates selection bias and can mistake noise for a pattern. Rerunning the same data adds no independent evidence. Test on unseen data and account for the search process.

prompts.story: Our Tuesday trades use inventory figures first published on Wednesday. The backtest earns 25% a year.
prompts.stem: What critical error remains even before trading costs are considered?

options.text: Weekly releases cannot be used in any trading strategy.
Every backtest above 20% annual return is invalid.
Tuesday's decisions use information first made public on Wednesday.
Trading on Tuesdays inherently creates survivorship bias.

prompts.why: First published on Wednesday fixes the earliest availability time. Using it on Tuesday is look-ahead bias. Align signals with actual release times; switching to monthly data does not automatically fix it.

prompts.story: Funds still operating today returned 9% a year over the last decade. We excluded funds that closed, so 9% represents the whole industry.
prompts.stem: How should the sample be repaired to assess industry returns?

options.text: Add only the largest funds that still operate.
Include historical returns of funds that closed during the period.
Keep the same list but shorten the window to one year.
Remove negative-return years from the current list.

prompts.why: Still operating today conditions inclusion on survival. Excluded funds may have performed worse, biasing the estimate upward. Restore the historical population, including closed funds, rather than adding more survivors.

prompts.story: We tested 100 ineffective factors, each with a correctly sized 5% significance test. Finding five significant results would establish five real effects.
prompts.stem: If every factor is ineffective, what is the expected number of false positives?

options.text: Zero: an ineffective factor cannot be significant.
One: only one hypothesis can be tested at a time.

prompts.why: A round trip has two sides: 12 minus 4 minus 4 equals 4 basis points. Eight deducts only one side. One basis point is 0.01 percentage point; all figures here use the same trade notional.

prompts.story: A buy signal occurs at $100, but the order fills at $100.30. The backtest books the buy at $100 because commissions are already included.
prompts.stem: How much adverse buy slippage relative to the signal price is omitted?

options.text: Zero, because commission is already included.
3 basis points, because the price gap is $0.30.
300 basis points, because the fill is above $100.

prompts.why: The buy fills above the signal price: $0.30 divided by $100 is 0.003, or 0.30%, which is 30 basis points. Commission and execution-price slippage are different costs; including one does not include the other.

prompts.story: We model three scenarios with returns of +12%, +4%, and −8%. No probabilities are assigned. The expected return is therefore 2.67%.
prompts.stem: What is missing when this scenario average is called an expected return?

options.text: Scenario probabilities and an account of which outcomes the scenarios cover.
Simply remove the negative scenario to obtain an expectation.
Simply add the three returns without dividing by three.
Having more than two scenarios automatically makes them equally likely.

prompts.why: (12% plus 4% minus 8%) divided by three is about 2.67%, an equal-weight scenario average. An expectation requires probability weights. Scenarios that omit possible outcomes also cannot directly establish the overall expected return.

prompts.story: The model estimates one-day 95% VaR at 2.1% of NAV. Therefore, a daily loss greater than 2.1% is impossible.
prompts.stem: Which reading matches this VaR estimate?

options.text: 2.1% is the largest possible daily loss under all conditions.
Under the model, about 5% of days exceed the threshold; tail-loss size is unspecified.
Exactly one day in every future block of twenty must lose exactly 2.1%.
95% means a 95% probability of making a profit.

prompts.why: 95% VaR estimates a loss quantile, not a hard loss cap or a fixed schedule of exceptions. It does not say how large losses beyond 2.1% can be. Actual exception rates can also differ if the model is inaccurate.

prompts.story: A correctly calibrated continuous-loss model estimates one-day 95% VaR. Over 250 trading days, no losses should exceed VaR because it is a risk limit.
prompts.stem: Under the stated model assumptions, about how many VaR exceedance days are expected?

options.text: 12.5 days: an expectation, not a required realized count.
Zero days: VaR is a hard ceiling that cannot be breached.
237.5 days: 95% of days must exceed the threshold.
Five days: 95% confidence directly means five days.

prompts.why: 250 times (1 minus 95%) gives 12.5 expected exceedance days, not a fixed schedule or a realized half-day. VaR is a quantile estimate. Exceptions alone do not establish model failure; assess frequency, clustering and tail stress too.

prompts.story: Annual net return is +4% at 5 basis points of slippage per trade, +1% at 10, and −2% at 15, with everything else fixed. Only the 5-basis-point case is highlighted as robust.
prompts.stem: What should be done before judging robustness?

options.text: Keep only the five-basis-point assumption because it gives the best result.
Average the three cases equally to prove future returns will be positive.
Display monthly returns so the negative number looks smaller.
Check realistic execution costs and disclose the assumptions under which returns turn negative.

prompts.why: The sensitivity analysis shows that changing slippage reverses the sign. Check which execution costs are realistic before judging robustness. Highlighting only the optimistic scenario hides the strategy's dependence on the cost assumption.
